review_note: Keep the concrete Tuesday, ledger, pressure column and permission to choose. Cut repeated declarations of the course’s stance and turn predicted classroom results into questions. Distinguish the recovery-hours planning device from research on time spent camouflaging.

edits.before:
You don't have to take that on the course's word. Bradley, Shaw, Baron-Cohen
and Cassidy surveyed **277 autistic adults**, in a survey designed in
partnership with autistic adults, and one of the three themes they found was
**"positive aspects of camouflaging"**: greater **access to social spaces**,
and **protection from harm**. Their summary of it is blunter than anything
this course would presume to write --- camouflaging was "seen as necessary to
survive in a world designed for the neurotypical majority" (Bradley et al.,
2021).

That is why there is no version of this lecture that tells you to stop.
edits.after:
Bradley, Shaw, Baron-Cohen and Cassidy surveyed **277 autistic adults**, in a
survey designed in partnership with autistic adults. One of the three themes
was **"positive aspects of camouflaging"**: greater **access to social
spaces**, and **protection from harm**. Camouflaging was "seen as necessary to
survive in a world designed for the neurotypical majority" (Bradley et al.,
2021).
edits.reason: Let the participants’ account carry the point; the previous paragraph already states the course’s position.

edits.before:
This ledger is denominated in **recovery hours**. That was a guess when it was
written. It is the right axis.
edits.after:
The ledger uses **recovery hours** to help plan the time you may need
alongside those demands. That remains a course planning device: time spent
camouflaging and time needed to recover are different quantities. This study
does not give a conversion between them.
edits.reason: Do not present a study of time spent camouflaging as validation of a recovery-time measure; retain the ledger and its stated planning status.

edits.before:
The switching finding is the one to hold on to. Changing how much you mask,
between the tutorial and the corridor, or between home and work, carries its own
charge. That goes in the ledger as a separate line.
edits.after:
Give switching its own line in the ledger. Estimate what changing how much
you mask costs you between the tutorial and the corridor, or between home and
work.
edits.reason: Give the practical instruction without announcing the finding’s importance or turning an association into a fixed individual charge.

edits.before:
So the whole room runs some managed performance. What differs is the price.
The same subroutine, sustained eye contact for a whole tutorial, costs one
person almost nothing and another person the rest of their afternoon. The lab
measures exactly that. Neither price is the correct one. Different
implementations pay different amounts for the same output.
edits.after:
Managed performance occurs across diagnostic groups. Its cost can differ:
sustained eye contact for a whole tutorial might cost one person almost nothing
and another the rest of their afternoon. In the lab you'll compare your own
estimates. Neither person's estimate sets the price for the other.
edits.reason: Keep the mixed-room argument and concrete example without predicting what every person does or what the lab will prove.

edits.before:
Most pairs find they disagree on the cost of the same subroutine by a factor of
two or more. That disagreement is the week.
edits.after:
How close were your estimates? If they differed, what might account for the
difference?
edits.reason: Replace invented classroom results with questions the activity can actually answer.
